prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (CNN) -- President Cristina Fernandez on Tuesday defended an increase in export taxes on grains that has riled many farmers, and she called on them to respect the law in protesting her policies. President Cristina Fernandez: Calls on rally Wednesday to support her policies. "All my life I have soldiered in this party, which always believed in social justice, in the redistribution of income, which caused us to win and lose elections," she said in a nationally televised address from the presidential palace. "But we were always respectful of the popular will." Fernandez, of the center-left Peronist movement, made her plea for comity a day after massive demonstrations in various cities blocked traffic and paralyzed much of the country. In a concession to her critics, Fernandez said the increase in taxes on exports of grains that she instituted in March by decree will be debated by Congress. But there is little likelihood that the Congress will order major changes, since her party controls both houses. But Hilda Duhalde, an opponent of Fernandez, was not persuaded. "It's true that they have a majority in both houses, but we have to put white on black and watch out for the small- and medium-sized producers, who are the ones suffering," she said. Argentina raised export taxes in March by more than 10 percent. Fernandez has said growers have benefited from rising world prices and the profits should be spread to help the poor. Farmers have countered that they need to reinvest the profits and that the higher taxes make it difficult for them to make a living. Fernandez said she was open to dialogue, but a dialogue that does not countenance the blocking of roads or other disruptions to the lives of Argentines. "Democracy for the people, not the corporations," she said. She called on Argentines to take to the Plaza de Mayo Wednesday in a show of support for her policies. "It doesn't matter what party, place or sector you're from," she said. "What is important is not where you're from, but where you are going -- what kind of country do we want?" To those who do not agree with her policies, she had other advice. "If they want to change the economic model, what they should do is organize a political party, participate in elections and win them," she said. CNN's Carolina Cayazzo contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (CNN) — President Cristina Fernandez on Tuesday defended an increase in grain export taxes that has angered many farmers and called on protesters to respect the law while opposing her policies.

President Cristina Fernandez called for a rally Wednesday in support of her policies.

“All my life, I have soldiered in this party, which has always believed in social justice and the redistribution of income—principles that have caused us to win and lose elections,” she said in a nationally televised address from the presidential palace. “But we were always respectful of the popular will.”

Fernandez, a member of the center-left Peronist movement, appealed for civility a day after massive demonstrations in several cities blocked traffic and paralyzed much of the country.

In a concession to her critics, Fernandez said the increase in grain export taxes, which she instituted by decree in March, would be debated by Congress. However, there is little likelihood that Congress will order major changes because her party controls both houses.

Hilda Duhalde, an opponent of Fernandez, was not persuaded.

“It’s true that they have a majority in both houses, but we have to put white on black and watch out for the small- and medium-sized producers, who are the ones suffering,” she said.

Argentina raised export taxes by more than 10 percent in March. Fernandez has said growers have benefited from rising world prices and that their profits should be shared to help the poor. Farmers have countered that they need to reinvest those profits and that the higher taxes make it difficult for them to earn a living.

Fernandez said she was open to dialogue, but not to a dialogue that countenanced roadblocks or other disruptions to the lives of Argentines.

“Democracy for the people, not the corporations,” she said.

She called on Argentines to gather in the Plaza de Mayo on Wednesday in a show of support for her policies.

“It doesn’t matter what party, place or sector you’re from,” she said. “What is important is not where you’re from, but where you are going—what kind of country do we want?”

For those who disagree with her policies, she offered other advice.

“If they want to change the economic model, what they should do is organize a political party, participate in elections and win them,” she said.

CNN’s Carolina Cayazzo contributed to this report.

**BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (CNN) —** Argentine President Cristina Fernandez defended higher grain-export duties Tuesday amid strong opposition from farmers and urged demonstrators to obey the law.

During a nationally broadcast speech from the presidential palace, Fernandez said she had spent her life working within a political movement committed to social justice and redistributing wealth—principles that had led the party to both electoral victories and defeats. She added that the movement had always honored the will of voters.

Fernandez, a member of the center-left Peronist movement, appealed for calm one day after large protests in several cities disrupted traffic and brought much of Argentina to a standstill.

As a concession to opponents, she announced that Congress would consider the grain-export tax increase she imposed by decree in March. Significant revisions appear unlikely, however, because her party holds majorities in both legislative chambers.

Opposition figure Hilda Duhalde remained unconvinced. She acknowledged that the government controls both houses but said the issue must be clearly examined, with particular attention paid to small and medium-sized agricultural producers, whom she described as those bearing the greatest burden.

Argentina increased grain-export taxes by more than 10% in March. Fernandez has argued that farmers have profited from rising global commodity prices and that some of those gains should be redistributed to assist poor people. Producers say they must put their earnings back into their businesses and that the increased taxes threaten their ability to earn a living.

The president said she was willing to hold talks, but not under circumstances involving roadblocks or other actions that interfere with Argentines’ daily lives. She framed the dispute as a choice between democracy serving ordinary citizens and power serving corporations.

Fernandez urged supporters, regardless of their political affiliation, region or social sector, to gather Wednesday in Buenos Aires’ Plaza de Mayo to demonstrate support for her agenda. She said the central question was not people’s origins but their shared destination and the kind of nation they wanted to build.

She also told those seeking a different economic approach that they should form a political party, compete in elections and win office.

CNN’s Carolina Cayazzo contributed to this report.

President Cristina Fernandez defended Argentina’s increase in grain export taxes as a necessary measure to redistribute income and provide greater support for the country’s poor. She argued that the policy would allow the government to direct more revenue toward social needs and reduce economic inequality.

The tax increase, however, provoked strong opposition from farmers. Agricultural producers organized demonstrations, blocked major roads, and disrupted transportation and commercial activity across the country. Critics maintained that the higher taxes would place an especially heavy burden on small- and medium-sized producers. Farmers also argued that retaining a reasonable share of their profits was essential for reinvesting in equipment, maintaining production, and sustaining their livelihoods.

In response to the unrest, Fernandez agreed to submit the export tax policy to Congress for debate and approval. Nevertheless, because her party controlled both legislative chambers, significant changes to the measure appeared unlikely.

Fernandez called for the dispute to be resolved through lawful and peaceful dialogue, insisting that negotiations should take place without road blockades or other disruptive tactics. At the same time, she urged her supporters to gather in Buenos Aires’s Plaza de Mayo, turning the controversy into a broader public demonstration of support for her government and its economic policies.

Argentine President Cristina Fernández defended her government’s decision to raise grain export taxes by more than 10 percent, arguing that the measure was necessary to ensure that the benefits of soaring international commodity prices were shared across society. She said farmers had profited substantially from rising global demand and favorable prices, while the government had a responsibility to use part of that windfall to finance social programs, infrastructure, and assistance for poorer Argentines.

The tax increase provoked a prolonged confrontation with agricultural producers, who said higher duties threatened their livelihoods and unfairly treated a diverse sector as if all farmers were wealthy. Rural organizations organized strikes, demonstrations, and road blockades, disrupting the transportation of grain and other goods. The protests also contributed to shortages and heightened political tensions in cities.

Fernández urged farm leaders to pursue their demands through legal and democratic channels rather than through actions that interfered with commerce and daily life. While defending the policy, she offered to send the measure to Congress for debate, presenting the move as an opportunity for elected representatives to consider the dispute openly.

The concession, however, appeared unlikely to result in major changes. Fernández’s governing party and its allies controlled Congress, making approval of the higher export taxes probable. Farm groups therefore remained skeptical that the legislative debate would produce a meaningful compromise.

The conflict remained unresolved, exposing a deeper divide over how Argentina should distribute the gains from its powerful agricultural sector. For the government, export taxes were a tool for reducing inequality and protecting the broader economy. For farmers, they represented an excessive burden imposed without adequate consultation. The dispute also raised wider questions about the limits of protest, the government’s response to dissent, and the role of democratic institutions in settling conflicts between national economic goals and rural livelihoods.

## Buenos Aires, Argentina

Buenos Aires, the vibrant capital of Argentina, is famous for its European-inspired architecture, energetic nightlife, and rich cultural heritage. Often called the “Paris of South America,” the city blends elegant boulevards and historic neighborhoods with a distinctly Latin American spirit.

Visitors can explore colorful La Boca, admire grand buildings in Recoleta, or enjoy cafés and boutiques in Palermo. Plaza de Mayo, the Casa Rosada, and the Teatro Colón are among the city’s most iconic landmarks. Buenos Aires is also the birthplace of tango, a passionate dance that can be experienced in traditional halls and lively street performances.

Food is central to local life. Argentine steak, empanadas, and dulce de leche are popular specialties, while sharing mate reflects the country’s warm social culture. With its creativity, history, and welcoming atmosphere, Buenos Aires offers an unforgettable introduction to Argentina.

**Argentine president defends grain export taxes amid farmer protests**

**BUENOS AIRES, Argentina** — Argentine President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner defended higher grain export taxes Tuesday as farmers continued nationwide protests that have disrupted food supplies and blocked major highways.

The government says the sliding-scale taxes on soybean, corn, wheat and sunflower exports are needed to control domestic food prices and redistribute profits from Argentina’s booming agricultural sector. The measure raised the soybean export levy from 35% to roughly 44% at prevailing prices.

Fernández said the farmers’ strike reflected the interests of a prosperous sector benefiting from high global commodity prices. She criticized rural leaders for organizing roadblocks and refusing to negotiate while the protests continued.

Farm organizations argue that the tax increase is excessive and threatens smaller producers already facing rising fuel, fertilizer and transportation costs. Farmers have halted grain and livestock sales and set up roadblocks across the country, leaving some supermarkets short of meat, dairy products and other staples.

The dispute has also triggered demonstrations in Buenos Aires, including nighttime protests by residents banging pots and pans. Government supporters have staged rival rallies.

Argentina is one of the world’s largest exporters of soybeans, corn and wheat, making the standoff a concern for international commodity markets. Rural groups say protests will continue unless the government suspends the new tax system and opens negotiations.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the political conflict in Argentina over Cristina Fernandez’s March increase in grain export taxes, including her televised remarks, the farmers’ objections, and the planned Plaza de Mayo rally.
counterfactuals.output:
In March 2008, President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner introduced a sliding-scale export tax that raised levies on soybeans and sunflower seeds as global prices climbed—pushing the soybean rate from about 35% to roughly 44%. Her government said the measure would capture windfall profits, restrain domestic food prices and finance redistribution.

Farm organizations responded with a nationwide sales strike and road blockades. They argued the tax was excessive or “confiscatory,” ignored rising costs, harmed smaller producers, and allowed the state to take most of the benefit from high commodity prices.

In a televised address, Fernández refused to reverse the policy, accused farm leaders of trying to pressure or “extort” the government, and contrasted their “pickets of abundance” with protests by impoverished Argentines during the 2001 crisis. Those remarks further inflamed the dispute and prompted anti-government demonstrations.

Government supporters, including Peronist organizations and unions, then planned a large rally in Buenos Aires’s Plaza de Mayo to demonstrate backing for Fernández and frame the conflict as a broader struggle over income redistribution and presidential authority.

Farm groups have staged strikes and blocked highways to protest increases in export duties, particularly on soybeans and other grains. The demonstrations have disrupted food deliveries and raised concerns about shortages in Buenos Aires and other cities.

Fernandez said farmers had the right to express their opposition but warned that roadblocks and other actions affecting the public could not be allowed to continue outside the law.

“No sector can place itself above the interests of the country,” she said in a televised address, defending the taxes as a way to distribute the benefits of Argentina’s agricultural boom and help control domestic food prices.

The president also appealed to labor unions, political organizations and other allies to support her administration, portraying the conflict as a test of policies intended to promote economic growth and social equality.

Farm leaders said the tax increases would sharply reduce producers’ income and accused the government of failing to consult the agricultural sector. They vowed to continue their protest unless officials reconsidered the measures.

The confrontation has become one of the most serious political challenges facing Fernandez since she took office in December 2007, succeeding her husband, former President Nestor Kirchner.

counterfactuals.output:
**Fernández sends disputed grain tax to Congress**

Argentine President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner sent her government’s controversial increase in grain-export taxes to Congress in June 2008, seeking legislative backing after months of farm strikes, roadblocks and political confrontation.

The administration’s Peronist coalition held majorities in both chambers, making approval appear likely. But the move exposed divisions within Peronism. Senator Hilda “Chiche” Duhalde, wife of former president Eduardo Duhalde, criticized the tax policy and warned that Congress should not simply rubber-stamp the executive’s decision.

The dispute centered on a sliding-scale export levy introduced in March, which raised the state’s share of revenues from soybeans and other crops as international prices climbed. Fernández argued that the measure would capture extraordinary farm profits, help redistribute wealth, restrain domestic food prices and finance social programs and infrastructure.

Farm organizations countered that the levies were excessive and, in some cases, confiscatory. They said the government overstated producers’ profits by ignoring rising costs, regional differences and the vulnerability of small and medium-sized farms. Critics also warned that the tax would discourage investment and production.

By referring the measure to Congress, Fernández sought to strengthen its democratic legitimacy without immediately withdrawing it. The decision shifted the conflict from highways and public rallies to the legislature, while leaving unresolved the broader struggle over how Argentina should divide the gains from its agricultural export boom.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a detailed CNN wire story on Argentina’s farm crisis, incorporating quotations from Cristina Fernandez about social justice, democracy, road blockades, elections, and the country’s economic model.
counterfactuals.output:
**Argentina’s farm crisis deepens as Fernandez defends taxes, challenges road blockades**

*By CNN*

**BUENOS AIRES, Argentina** — Argentina’s confrontation with its powerful farm sector has escalated into one of the gravest political crises of President Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner’s administration, disrupting food supplies, blocking highways and exposing a deeper argument over democracy, social justice and the direction of Latin America’s third-largest economy.

Farm organizations began strikes and road blockades after Fernandez’s government introduced a sliding-scale export tax in March 2008, raising levies on soybeans and other commodities as international prices climbed. Producers say the measure, known as Resolution 125, is confiscatory and threatens the survival of smaller farms. The government says the revenue is essential to redistribute the gains from Argentina’s commodities boom and prevent domestic food prices from following world markets higher.

Fernandez has framed the dispute as a test of the economic model built after Argentina’s devastating 2001-02 financial collapse.

“This is not a fight against the countryside,” she said in a nationally televised address as the confrontation intensified. Instead, she argued, the conflict centers on how the extraordinary income generated by high commodity prices should be shared across a country still marked by poverty and inequality.

The president has repeatedly described the export-tax policy as an instrument of **social justice**, saying the state has a responsibility to channel part of the agricultural sector’s windfall toward workers, pensioners and poorer provinces.

“Redistribution of income is the key to social justice,” Fernandez said, defending an economic strategy that combines government intervention, a competitive currency, subsidies and taxes on exports.

### Road blockades strain cities

The farm groups’ principal weapon has been the blockade of major highways. Protesters have stopped trucks carrying grain and livestock, while at various stages allowing private vehicles and other traffic to pass. The demonstrations have nevertheless caused shortages of meat, milk and produce in Buenos Aires and other urban centers.

Fernandez condemned the tactics, drawing a sharp distinction between lawful protest and actions that restrict the movement of food and goods.

“I ask you, in the name of all Argentines, to clear the roads,” she said.

In an earlier speech, she derided some of the demonstrations as **“pickets of abundance,”** contrasting them with the road protests staged by unemployed Argentines during the economic crisis. The phrase inflamed tensions in farming communities, where producers said the government was portraying a diverse sector — including thousands of tenants and smallholders — as a uniformly wealthy elite.

Rural leaders responded that blockades were among the few tools available to force negotiations with a government they accused of imposing the new tax without consultation. They also argued that farmers already bear high transport, fuel and fertilizer costs and receive little in return in rural infrastructure.

The conflict has divided Argentina geographically and politically. Large rallies supporting farmers have been held in agricultural provinces, while government supporters, trade unions and social movements have mobilized in Buenos Aires.

### Democracy and the authority of elections

Fernandez, who won the presidency in October 2007 and took office in December, has invoked her electoral mandate in responding to pressure from the streets.

“Governments are chosen through elections,” she said, emphasizing that policies should be debated through democratic institutions rather than decided by road blockades or economic pressure.

She has also insisted that protest groups cannot claim authority equal to that of an elected government. “No sector can place itself above the law or above the will of the people,” Fernandez said.

Her comments reflect one of the central political questions raised by the crisis: whether the farm organizations are exercising a legitimate democratic right to protest or using their control over production and transport routes to overturn a policy adopted by a constitutionally elected administration.

Opposition politicians have accused Fernandez of deepening the divide with combative rhetoric. They say winning an election does not eliminate the government’s obligation to consult affected sectors or to seek compromise.

Fernandez, however, has argued that democracy involves more than voting and must also produce greater equality.

“Democracy is not only the right to vote,” she said. “It must also mean the possibility of living better, with education, health and work.”

### Debate over the economic model

The farm crisis has become a referendum on the Kirchner economic program, first pursued by Fernandez’s husband and predecessor, Nestor Kirchner.

After defaulting on roughly $100 billion in debt and abandoning the peso’s one-to-one link with the U.S. dollar, Argentina experienced several years of rapid growth. A weaker currency encouraged exports, while high prices for soybeans and other commodities filled government coffers.

The administration used export taxes and other revenue to finance subsidies, public works, pension increases and social programs. Supporters credit the model with reviving industry, creating jobs and restoring state authority after the collapse.

“Our economic model is one of production, employment and social inclusion,” Fernandez said. “It is a model that has allowed millions of Argentines to recover work and dignity.”

Critics say that model has become increasingly dependent on commodity revenue and discretionary state spending. Economists have also warned that high inflation, price controls, unreliable official statistics and energy shortages could erode Argentina’s gains.

Soybeans sit at the center of the argument. Argentina is one of the world’s leading producers and exporters of soy products, and the crop has expanded dramatically across the fertile Pampas. The government says higher export duties capture part of the benefit generated by international prices and the competitive exchange rate.

Farmers counter that the sliding tax rises too aggressively when prices increase and fails to distinguish adequately between large agribusiness operations and smaller producers far from ports.

### Congress becomes the battleground

Seeking a way out of the standoff, Fernandez sent the export-tax plan to Congress, saying lawmakers should decide its future. The move shifted the confrontation from rural highways and public plazas into the legislature, where the government’s coalition faced defections from representatives in farming provinces.

Fernandez presented that step as evidence that the dispute would be resolved democratically.

“Let Congress debate, let Congress decide,” she said. “That is democracy.”

The lower house narrowly approved the measure after an extended debate. But the Senate split evenly, leaving Vice President Julio Cobos — constitutionally the chamber’s presiding officer — to cast the deciding vote.

Cobos broke with Fernandez and voted against the government’s proposal, saying his conscience would not allow him to support it. His rejection delivered a dramatic political defeat to the president and exposed fractures inside the governing coalition.

The administration subsequently withdrew the contested tax system.

### Political costs likely to endure

Even with the immediate policy reversed, the conflict has left lasting damage. Fernandez’s approval ratings fell during the confrontation, and relations between the government and rural organizations remain deeply strained.

The crisis also demonstrated the political power of Argentina’s agricultural interior and the ability of farmers to build alliances with urban middle-class voters dissatisfied with inflation and the government’s confrontational style.

For Fernandez, the issue remains inseparable from the broader question of who benefits from Argentina’s growth.

“What is being discussed is the distribution of income,” she said. “What is being discussed is what kind of country we want.”

Farm leaders say they support national development and social programs but reject the suggestion that opposing Resolution 125 amounts to opposing solidarity. They are calling for differentiated tax rates, lower levies for small producers and greater investment in rural roads and transportation.

The dispute may have started over soybeans, but it has become a struggle over political legitimacy and Argentina’s post-crisis identity: whether economic power should be checked through aggressive state intervention, or whether the government has pushed redistribution beyond what producers and democratic institutions will accept.

With future elections looming, both sides know the argument will continue far beyond the highways and grain terminals. Fernandez’s government must defend its economic record while rebuilding support outside its urban and working-class base. The farm sector, meanwhile, must convert the influence gained during the blockades into a lasting political program.

For Argentines, the crisis has made one fact clear: The fertile land that powers the country’s exports is also the ground on which its most consequential political battles are being fought.

*Editor’s note: Quotations are translated from Spanish and should be checked against official transcripts or source video before publication.*
